headline: Commission approves trail plan alignments and agrees to serve as community garden appeal body
summary: The Commission accepted a consent agenda including special use permits and June minutes, heard updates on a proposed tree ordinance, trail system changes, Calahan Park court and pathway projects, and summer surveying findings. Members voted to support trail plan implementation and to take on the role of appeal body for the community garden program, pending a policy from staff.
decisions: Accepted the consent agenda, including special use permit requests for Burlington Greenway, Calahan Park, and Pomeroy Park, and the June minutes.
Supported implementation and alignment of the trail system plans presented for Leddy Park, Kieslich Park, Arms Forest, and Oakledge.
Agreed to serve as the appeal body for the Burlington Area Community Garden program, pending a policy and process from Parks staff.

decision_evidence.quote:
Davis made a motion to accept the consent agenda, Bergmann seconded.
All were in favor, none opposed.

Boehm made a motion to support the implementation and alignments needed to achieve the trail plans, Bergmann seconded. 
All were in favor, none opposed.

Boehm made a motion to accept the role of the appeal body for the BACG program for cases that require due process for participants of the program contingent on Parks staff providing a policy and process for the Commission to follow, Mobley seconded. 
All were in favor, none opposed.

plain_text:
Parks Commission Meeting 
August 11th, 2026 at 5:30pm 
645 Pine St., Front Conference Room & Zoom 
 
Staff in Attendance: Lewis, Sauve, Cahill, Comai, Schmidt, Madalinski, Gustin, Holmes & O’Daniel 
Commissioners in Attendance: Lantieri, Boehm, Mobley, Davis, Bergmann, Mamo & Etter 
 
Lantieri opened the meeting at 5:31pm by welcoming everyone and introducing the newest 
Commissioner, Frank Mamo.  
1. Agenda 
1.1 Motion to amend/adopt agenda 
Lantieri noted that there was one amendment to the agenda needed, which was to include 
the June minutes as an item to be approved with the Consent Agenda.  
Bergmann made a motion to amend the agenda to include the June minutes as an item to 
be approved with the Consent Agenda, Mobley seconded.  
All were in favor of the amended agenda, none opposed. 
 
2. Consent Agenda 
2.1 Burlington Greenway Special Use Permit Request (Old Spokes Home) 
2.2 Burlington Greenway Special Use Permit Request (Sarah Ramsey Strong 5K) 
2.3 Calahan Park Special Use Permit Request (GBGSL Fall) 
2.4 Pomeroy Park Special Use Permit (Momo’s Market) 
2.5 June minutes 
Davis made a motion to accept the consent agenda, Bergmann seconded. 
All were in favor, none opposed. 
 
3. Public Forum – Time Certain, 6pm 
3.1 Verbal Comments 
Public forum was opened at 6:02pm. 
Colin McNeil was present online and wanted to make a comment about Smalley Park. 
He shared that it doesn’t feel like it is being maintained and wanted to put in a request 
that the City keep this park in mind and keep maintaining the softball field so it is 
available for all users now and in the future and so that it doesn’t go into disrepair. 
Scott Gustin and Zoe Richards were present in person and noted that this was a sneak 
peek of an action item that will be in front of the Commission next month. Gustin began 
by sharing that they are talking to trust for public land about doing an ecosystem 
services analysis for Burlington.  
Richards introduced herself as a long-term member of the Conservation Board. She then 
explained that ecosystem services are a way of recognizing the value that many of the 
healthy ecosystems that are present within the City have, like street trees, wetlands and
functional forests, which is an infrastructure that we rely on as a City. She continued 
that they reduce storm water and air pollutants and keep us cool, among other things, 
and that there is a goal of calculating some of those benefits so that when an 
appropriate use for an open space is being discussed, there is a way of calculating what 
that value is. She shared the example that a relatively healthy ecosystem will absorb 
more stormwater than any built green stormwater infrastructure. She continued that it 
is really worth understanding what Burlington already has and what its value is, 
especially when trade-offs are needed when discussing how to approach open space, 
like when building is involved. This will be helpful for the important process of thinking 
about the value that natural systems and healthy ecosystems play within the City 
because it will allow for continued investment in those being healthy. Richards shared 
that nature-based climate solutions are one of the most impactful climate solutions that 
you can have for a City because it is things that people can really feel and see and 
understand, like dropping the temperature of the City by growing enough trees. She 
shared that she feels this will set the stage to continue to invest in the City’s existing 
healthy ecosystems. 
Gustin shared that ecosystem services are a recurring theme in both the new open 
space plan that was adopted earlier this year, but also in the 2022 nature-based climate 
solutions addendum, including a few action items related to execution and 
implementation of nature-based climate solutions and evaluation modification of those 
processes. He continued that this study will be looking in City-wide green spaces, which 
includes public, private and institutional properties including the core ecological areas 
like Rock Point and Arms Forest but also the green connective tissues through the 
neighborhoods and community at large. Gustin noted that fundamentally, it is about 
improved decision making for important decision making, like building more housing. He 
continued that by doing this study, it will give the City an opportunity to better 
understand and quantify the multiple public benefits of the open spaces and 
incorporate that information into future decision making. He shared that there are 2 
primary components to this study that they are anticipating: the economic benefits of 
open spaces and the climate cooling benefit of these green spaces throughout the 
community. Gustin then shared that there are 3 primary topic areas: humanities climate 
solutions, stormwater management and air quality. He concluded by explaining that 
they are hoping to fund this out of the Conservation Legacy Fund, for roughly $79,000, 
and will need the Commission’s approval to do so. 
Richards chimed in that this was something that the Planning Commission requested 
during the Open Space Plan planning process.  
Mobley asked if they felt this would be done in time to impact the Plan BTV work that is 
happening. 
Gustin and Richards answered yes.   
Public forum was closed at 6:12pm. 
 
4. Deliberative Agenda 
4.1 Tree Ordinance Update
Gustin began by sharing his screen with the current working draft of the tree and 
vegetation ordinance, noting that this was not an action item tonight, but another 
review of a draft that had been updated since the initial review by this body, the 
Conservation Board and City Council’s ordinance committee. He continued that there 
will be one more round of revisions before coming back as an action item for support for 
an adoption in September. He then went through the changes that were made by other 
bodies from the last draft. The highlights were that the authority section definitions 
were fleshed out a bit, the City Arborist and City Land Steward titles in regards to trees 
were solidified, definitions about climate resilience were added and definitions about 
different types of vegetation were discussed. 
Cahill noted that the introductions in the definitions were related to some pieces that 
were added around removing plant material from City property and then providing 
clarity around what that process is, which is coming up more and more in the realm of 
seed collection for native seeds to make sure there are enough for the birds, insects and 
natural processes as well as folks who are interested in growing from seed.  
Gustin continued that this part also provided more detailed provisions around removal, 
cutting and pruning vegetation and trees on public property. He shared that they also 
articulated the role of the Conservation Board a bit more and added in reviewing the 
annual goals and objectives prepared by the City Arborist and/or Land Steward and also 
serving as a public forum for the community around things like the ash tree 
management, for example. He continued that they fleshed out more detail around 
obstruction of streets, which he shared articulates the responsibilities for the private 
property owners who have trees or shrubs that are on public street right of ways with 
the potential of encroachment and enables follow-up and enforcement action to 
compel compliance in those instances. Gustin continued by touching on shade trees, 
which are a tree on public property planted by a public entity – like a street tree or a 
tree in a park, but not trees in public forests. He then mentioned an additional category 
called “other trees” that was added and noted that where zoning is involved, it refers to 
the comprehensive development ordinance. Gustin shared the final highlights that they 
worked out a bit more were mitigation measures or applications that include tree 
removal. He shared that if someone requests approval to remove a certain amount of 
trees and approval is given, there are mitigation measures on a caliper caliper basis. He 
used the example of someone removing 100 inches, which need to be replaced, which 
can happen on-site or off-site, and off-site requires a consultation with the Land 
Steward or City Arborist. He continued that if off-site is not feasible, a payment based 
on plant appraisal needs to be made into a tree fund. He shared that the other option is 
installing and maintaining on-site green infrastructure.   
Mobley asked if there was a storm event and someone were to lose trees in their yard, 
does this come into play in this scenario? 
Gustin answered no, only if someone sought approval to intentionally remove trees on 
private public and institution properties, with private property governed by the zoning 
code in this ordinance-based reference to that.  
Mamo asked if there was any consideration to change or review the way trees on public 
lands are reviewed or approached, noting that the removal of ash trees in the Old North
End altered the neighborhoods noticeably. He shared that he felt the communication 
from Parks about why they we removing the trees was excellent, but that it created a 
renewed understanding of how important trees in public spaces are, especially in the 
ONE where people don’t have large yards so most of the trees are public trees.   
Cahill answered that after the ash tree removal, there were lessons learned and space 
for adaptations to be made. He did note however, that adding complexity and process 
to work plans when the department and City are working with less resources and 
employees would be a challenge, but one worth meeting. 
Gustin noted that the process for removing shade trees is articulated in the state statute 
and a primary point in this ordinance is to provide a defined community process. 
Cahill chimed in that it also allows for it to be staff-led in the way that integrating the 
process with a body allows for diverse and robust dialogue. He feels there could also be 
space for community process and engagement with mourning the loss of trees, like 
honoring them with other plantings.  
Comai agreed that having a really active tree board on the Conservation Board will be 
helpful in the future to have an open public discussion about what the tree team is 
doing and for presenting their yearly plans and long-term goals. He continued that he 
has heard of communities who review every public tree that might be taken down and 
shared that this would not be helpful here. He shared that his team often runs into 
situations where there’s a storm-damaged tree and they make the decision on the spot 
when they respond to the call if the remainder of the tree needs to come down because 
it is a public safety issue. Comai continued by reflecting on how he and his team feel the 
impacts of all of the ash removal in the Old North End every day, noting that they’re out 
there caring for and growing the trees. He shared that they have been planning for this 
for 8 years and have been planting new trees ahead of removals as much as possible, 
including planting 214 trees in Wards 2 and 3, in addition to other trees since then 
across all of the Wards.  
Lantieri asked if his team is aware of where they will be planting and removing every 
year.  
Comai answered for the most part, yes, and that they have been very systematically 
removing ash trees since 2024, which included removing all of the ash in one area at the 
same time to streamline the process. He shared they are currently aware of some 
larger, older trees that looked okay last year but will need to come down this year due 
to drought conditions and sidewalk replacement work. He continued that outside of 
things like that, removals aren’t always known ahead of time, especially when storm or 
vehicle damage is involved. Comai shared that they do know in advance where they will 
be planting and shared that they currently have a list of 110 locations that could be 
planted this fall. He noted that their policy is to plant a new tree in a removal location 
within a calendar year if the site is viable. He closed by sharing that yes they have a work 
plan but it can change daily with incoming See Click Fixes and emergency calls 
consistently coming through.  
Lantieri thanked him and reiterated that the Tree Board will be a great venue to see 
what the work plan is while also understanding the pieces can that ebb and flow.
Gustin chimed in that the next step will be to update the draft to its final form to be 
approved by the Conservation Board, this body and then City Council, ideally in 
September and October.  
 
4.2 Trail System Review 
Cahill opened by sharing that the Department is on the cusp of kicking off some of our 
trail system maps of the parks and coming to this body to review system alignments 
with the trails has been a helpful step in this process. He noted that trails have been 
ranked highly as a beloved and vital asset within the part system, so anytime there is 
work being done to align those trails, forest stewardship and system development can 
come along with it, which is why giving the Commission a chance to be involved and ask 
questions is so important. He continued that while they’re not expecting controversy, 
but when and if there is community dialogue, having the support of a space where that 
can happen is helpful for the staff doing the work. Cahill noted that while this is a bit of 
alignment of a process it is also celebrating getting better wayfinding for the parks 
system. He closed by sharing that they plans in the packet were all guided by safety, 
sustainability and accessibility, which is how these trail system changes are developed. 
Schmidt introduced himself and explained that in his role as Conservation Field 
Coordinator, he oversees the natural areas and trails and conservation projects 
happening in those areas. He reiterated what Cahill noted about safety, accessibility and 
sustainability and shared that they don’t actively make changes to trail plans by looking 
through the lens of user conflict, unsafe conditions or ecologically unsustainable 
conditions, which all prompt trail changes. He continued that because they are doing 
this new wayfinding thing, they wanted to make sure there are trails that they want to 
put on maps and for people to know about. He then shared the Leddy Park map, noting 
that there are a lot of social trails that have bisected the 2 main trails. He noted that this 
is an area of user conflict so the hope is to take an area with old social trails and put a 
little more attention into it, recognizing that there are a lot of people who walk there 
but now there are a lot of bikers because of the bike park. He continued that they want 
to do work preemptively to make sure that each of the user groups feel like they have a 
space that is safe and accessible and where there can be different types of experiences 
on the trails. He continued that with all of this in mind, he is proposing 2 separate trails, 
a pedestrian and a multi-use trail, going the same directions and closing the little cross 
social trails to eliminate all of those intersections. He noted that this would involve 
minimal trail development, but give folks a nice option for walking. Schmidt then shared 
that something they do now when building trails is purposely slow the flow of traffic of 
all kinds, which is done so that multiple user groups can use the trail safely. He 
continued by noting that this is in a lower priority ecological zone of Leddy Park. 
Schmidt then brought everyone’s attention to another trail connecting to Leonard 
Street that community members have been asking for for a long time. He shared that he 
has been working with Madalinski from the Planning Team and that it would be an 
incredibly easy spot to put a trail in and it would be a really nice access point for the 
community. Schmidt then touched on Kieslich Park, noting that they will not be 
changing the trails that are present, but have rehabilitated some old social trails that
had become overgrown and will be adding in a wayfinding kiosk. Next he showed the 
Arms Forest map, noting that no changes will be made to this trail system either, but the 
already approved trails map will be on the kiosk that has been installed at the meadow.  
Mobley shared that Arms Forest was mentioned on her tour of the new high school, 
which she felt was extremely positive and exciting. 
Schmidt shared that he worked with a BHS YES class to rehabilitee the trail that runs 
from the high school into the forest, which was just a first step in more thoroughly 
integrating BHS students into that forest system and having them play a role in the 
stewardship of it.  
Cahill noted that there was some minimal disturbance to the forest during construction 
and the school district was great about working with us on how to restore different 
pieces of it. He continued that there’s aspirational intention to have students help with 
that restoration work over time.  
Schmidt continued by touching on Oakledge, noting that a majority of the social trails at 
Oakledge are not safe, accessible or sustainably built, so the goal is to close those, 
especially the really dangerous ones that are very steep and eroded. He continued that 
part of that process will involve making the safe trails that they want to make the official 
trails more inviting to encourage use of those instead.  
Davis asked how they close the social trails.  
Schmidt answered that closing a popular social trail is a work in progress and involves 
brushing in to discretely dissuade use over time. He continued that the other trail at 
Oakledge that goes from the upper parking lot through the meadow, is a great birding 
area and one of the few areas in Burlington that could actually be ADA accessible with a 
durable surface that has the right grades to actually accommodate a wheelchair. He 
noted that these trails exist already, but are often wet so putting in something like a 
gravel path would make them accessible in many different ways. He shared that the trail 
map that would be posted at the site would ideally include these for future use.  
Davis asked how this would all work with the budget. 
Lewis answered that the Conservation team has been very creative coming up with 
ways to make lemonade out of lemons. He continued that they have the funds that are 
available and maximize them to the best of their abilities utilizing the talents they have 
on their full-time team, seasonal staff and volunteers. He noted that the trail system is 
not as incorporated into the capital budget program as much as it probably should be, 
which was identified through the budgeting processes. He feels there is opportunity to 
tie in some of these efforts to make sure there are appropriate funds for the build out of 
these capital goods.  
Schmidt chimed in that everything in the proposal can be done in-house both by hand 
and machine, so it’s more a matter of time and what we don’t do when we do big 
projects like this.  
Cahill noted that the permitting piece will take time and is something that needs to be 
explored.  
Lantieri shared that this is all very exciting and could be a great opportunity to engage 
the public and volunteers.
Schmidt agreed, noting the positive experience so far with engaging the public in 
removing buckthorn from Oakledge Park.  
Boehm made a motion to support the implementation and alignments needed to 
achieve the trail plans, Bergmann seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed. 
 
4.3 Burlington Area Community Garden Program Appeal Body 
Cahill opened by sharing a brief history of the community garden program, noting that 
the first site was opened in 1972 at Oakledge park for 1 year and then the idea of 
community gardens took hold across the US through a private endeavor, Garden Way 
Carts, who created community gardens to help sell their products via newsletters. Cahill 
continued that Tommy Thompson’s efforts to create community gardens in the 
Burlington area came from these funds as a part of the back to the land movement, but 
were lacking any sort of longevity or infrastructure. He continued that eventually 
Garden Way got out of the business and they hired Larry Sommers from Eating Well 
Magazine helped these go from private endeavors to public, so in the early 80s it 
became a nonprofit that had a board. He shared that that board oversaw the 
community garden program for 4-5 years until they could not fund it anymore, and then 
Bernie Sanders, who was Burlington’s Mayor at the time, made it a program through the 
Parks and Recreation Department. Cahill continued that the board became an advisory 
board through the transition and especially during those early years making sure the 
City held its promise but over time as the City investment into the program was 
becoming stronger, especially when things turned the corner to having Meghan 
O’Daniel in her role supporting the gardens, the advisory board eventually chose to 
disband. He shared that this has not been felt for the most part – there is a robust 
network of site leaders that Meghan supports and coordinates, who act as a larger body 
of thought partners and community gardeners. Cahill noted, however, that one specific 
and important function was lost in the disbanding of the advisory board – being an 
appeal committee in the event that someone is disinvited from the program and that 
those individuals have due process to appeal those decisions made by staff. Cahill noted 
that this is a very rare occurrence and we do our best to work with folks before it gets to 
this point, but are realizing this is a bit of a gap in the process and sometimes the 
conversation needs to extend beyond staff. He concluded that we are looking to the 
Parks Commission to provide that function in the event that there is an appeal where a 
gardener could come before you and be heard, which would put the board in a place to 
render a final decision.  
Mobley asked if this had been run through legal. She also noted that this would provide 
a point of engagement, albeit somewhat challenging, which has been a goal of the 
current commission and there is value in that. She also shared curiosity about potential 
training opportunities in mediation for Commissioners to be able to participate in this 
comfortably.  
Boehm felt that this was a good idea and agreed that there should be more process 
figured out. She then asked if there are other examples of this in other aspects of the 
City that could be referenced.
The group then discussed potential frameworks and policy for this process and the 
general agreement was to check in with the City Attorney’s office next.   
Davis asked how many site leaders there are and if they get paid.  
Cahill answered that there are around 30 because we encourage more than 1 per site 
and they do not get paid.  
Davis asked if they were the people monitoring the plots.  
Cahill answered that yes, they are the first line of interpretation of the plot maintenance 
policy.  
Mamo asked how often this happens.  
Cahill answered maybe 3 times in the last 15 years. 
The group then discussed how to proceed – noting that they are open to taking on this 
responsibility but would like to have this brought to the City Attorney’s office and have a 
policy in place. 
Boehm made a motion to accept the role of the appeal body for the BACG program for 
cases that require due process for participants of the program contingent on Parks staff 
providing a policy and process for the Commission to follow, Mobley seconded.  
All were in favor, none opposed.  
 
4.4 Calahan Park – Upcoming Updates 
Madalinski began by explaining that he was at the meeting to give the Commission 
some updates on projects in different stages of design completion that are expected to 
go into construction at Calahan Park in the next year. He began by speaking to the 
courts, sharing that they put out an RFP in the spring of 2025 for the design of a 
bioretention basin, the reconstruction of the basketball and tennis courts and a tree 
trench stormwater feature that would go in between the two sets of courts, all of which 
were in the comprehensive plan. He continued that around the same time, the 
department applied for an LWCF grant with the hopes that it would fund all of this, 
which was expected to cost roughly in the $1.2 million range. He then shared that after 
they got through their contracting and had the design engineer onboard, they learned 
that they had not gotten the LWCF grant and the official cost estimate came back at 
closer to $2 million. All of this resulted in the Planning Team peeling back pieces that the 
comprehensive plan had initially included, like a large retaining wall near the basketball 
courts and all of the stormwater pieces, and taking them out of the scope. He continued 
that this led them to potentially building just 1 basketball court instead of 2. Madalinski 
also shared that they also did some creative moving around of bond funds so that all of 
the courts can still be built at the same time and to hopefully put lighting in for each of 
them. He continued that by peeling back the scope like they did, they are more in the 
$700k to $800k range now and they’re just about ready to bring the drawings forward 
for permitting and to submit them to the zoning department. Because Madalinski was 
not able to share his screen, he then described what was included on the drawing he 
had been hoping to share: moving and building 1 basketball court with 10’ fencing 
around it that would be lit, a connecting pathway between the basketball and tennis 
courts that connects to the new entrance, grading to make everything ADA accessible, 
one of the sets of 4 tennis courts will be converted into pickleball courts and all of the
tennis/pickleball courts will be lit and controlled by a timer. Madalinski shared his hope 
for feedback and thoughts on outreach to the community, especially about the lighting 
and noise considerations that go along with that.  
Mobley suggested tabling at events to help get the information out could be a good 
approach and noted that doing this outreach is a good idea.  
Madalinski then gave an update about the Calahan pathway, sharing that after hearing 
from neighbors about the various trees that were planned for removal, they worked 
with their design engineer and BED to make some changes so now the sugar maple, 
Norway maple and the pine tree next to the playground will remain. He noted that the 
pine tree will need to have some limbing done and BED will need to do some additional 
work to put another pole in and relocating some cables.  
Lantieri shared that he feels the community will be pleased to hear that you all are 
responding to their feedback.  
 
4.5 Commission Members & Ward Distribution 
Lantieri asked everyone to share what Ward they were in.  
Davis said she was in Ward 4. 
Lantieri, Boehm, Bergmann, Mobley and Etter said they were in Ward 5. 
Mamo said he was in Ward 2. 
 
4.6 Comprehensive Plan Update (Intern Surveying Overview) 
Holmes introduced herself, sharing that she was one of the Parks Planning interns, and 
explaining that she would be presenting the Commission with an update on what they 
have been up to this summer. She continued that they have been gathering community 
input in parks in support of PlanBTV 2050, specifically in regards to the revision of the 
BPRW comprehensive plan, which fits into that, noting that they especially focused on 
the waterfront (Starr Farm, Oakledge and Waterfront Parks) which did not get an in 
depth look for the 2015 plan. She then shared that over the course of 10 weeks they 
conducted 15 minute passerby counts in those locations and on the Greenway, noting 
whether people were passive or active and their demographics. This enabled them to 
model an average week day and weekend day in each of these locations from 8am – 
8pm. She shared that they also conducted 175 interviews in these parks and at events in 
other locations to gather more individual feedback. Homes then noted their guiding 
questions – who is using the parks, how do people use the parks and what do people 
love the most about the parks/what do they wish was different? She then shared some 
of their findings: toddlers, youth and seniors were overrepresented in comparison to 
the overall demographics of BTV, seniors were equally distributed amongst the locations 
while toddlers and youth were more present at Oakledge and Starr Farm, Oakledge had 
two times as many passive park users than active while Starr Farm mainly had active 
users, people spent more time at Oakledge than other parks with over 80% of survey 
respondents there saying they planned to spend over an hour at the park, more people 
at Oakledge and Starr Farm were coming from home compared to a higher number of 
people treating Waterfront Park as more of a stop in their day instead of the 
destination, around 60% of the people at Waterfront Park were from out of town
(destination location) with people from 15 states represented and some people from 
Canada as well, and over half of the people at Oakledge were from out of town but 
relatively close by (regional park) while 80% of people surveyed at Starr Farm were from 
the New North End (neighborhood park). Holmes then polled the group to see which 
park they thought had the most visitors, the answer being Oakledge. She then shared a 
graph of the number of visitors to each park by the hour as well as a different graph 
showing how people got to the parks noting that Oakledge had the most people who 
came by car, Starr Farm had the most people who came through their own power 
(biking/walking) and Waterfront had the most different modes of transport, including 
public transit and boat. Holmes continued that with this data, a deeper picture of each 
park and how they are used can be painted. She reiterated that Oakledge tends to have 
younger users engaged in passive activities and is used more like a regional destination 
for things like swimming, picnics and lawn games, while Waterfront Park is used like an 
extension of downtown and functions more like a square or a plaza for visitors to 
Burlington and Starr Farm is used as a neighborhood park for New North End residents. 
She summarized that changes to the parks should begin with recognizing what they 
already are and how they are used and can be used to make informed decisions and 
help determine how to spend resources. Holmes then touched on comment themes 
throughout the process, noting that most comments were positive and the ones that 
were negative were mostly about unhoused people in parks, but with the understanding 
of the complexity of the problem. Homes then shared that Greenway users shared that 
they felt it was a “treasure” and a “critical resource for the city”. Homes then shared 
that people were overall very happy with the recreational facilities available and felt a 
sense of community through events such as Juneteenth and Leddy Beach Bites. She 
mentioned that many people were interested in more bathrooms and waterfrountains 
throughout the park system. Holmes then shared some direct quotes from folks 
surveyed and what it was like to interact with people in the parks over the summer. She 
then shared that their next step will be synthesizing this data and writing a report so 
that it can be used by the Department.  
The Commissioners shared their excitement about this process and the data gathered.  
 
5. Standing Items 
5.1 Parks Foundation Update 
Lantieri noted that the Pomeroy playground opening happened, which was a big 
milestone for the Parks Foundation and their Playgrounds for All campaign. He then 
shared that they are a separate non-profit that raises money specifically for park 
projects, and in this case, playground equipment. He continued that the Parks 
Commission has a member that attends their meetings, which he has been doing, but he 
became an official member of the Parks Foundation at the last meeting so he asked 
others to consider being the Parks Commissioner who attends. Lantieri then asked if 
anyone attended the Pomeroy playground opening. 
Lewis shared that he attended and that it went well with a lot of positive feedback and 
energy. He thanked the YMCA for joining the event and bringing children over to use the
new playground. He gave kudos to the Planning Team for putting all of those efforts 
together.  
Mamo shared that he attended the opening and that he and his family use that 
playground and park daily.  
Lantieri thanked all who were involved and thanked the Parks Foundation for the 
generous donation that made it happen and for continuing to fund the Playgrounds for 
All campaign. 
 
5.2 Director’s Report 
Lewis referenced the report and also highlighted the City’s July 3rd event, BPRW and 
PACC engagement with the resolution that was recently passed at City Council, 
additional conversations in the Ordinance committee around e-motos and measures 
that staff are taking in the field, summer programming wrapping up and fall 
programming starting soon and that there will hopefully be a Leddy Manager hired 
soon.  
Mobley noted that in reference to the Burlington Forward resolution, she feels that 
there is a juxtaposition that she understands but hopes that the cuts that were made to 
the department in 2025, which were deep and impactful, are not forgotten as 
engagement and responsibilities are potentially being added with fewer resources to 
support what is already being done. She continued that she hopes there will be space to 
have bigger conversations about this.  
Lewis shared his appreciation for that and noted that he’s confident that the Council 
recognizes that and is taking that into consideration. 
 
5.3 Commissioner’s Items & Volunteer Hours 
Lantieri shared that he’s been focused on volunteer engagement and will be meeting 
with Cahill and O’Daniel later this week. He had 25 hours to report since the last 
meeting. 
Davis had 3 hours to report visiting parks, gardens and the bike path. 
Etter had 1.5 hours to report.
